chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Najran, from Asim ibn Humayn Humayd, from Abi Baseer, from Abi Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) sent Ali (peace be upon him) to Yemen, so he (peace be upon him) said to him (peace be upon him) when he returned: 'Tell me the most wondrous thing that came to you.' He (peace be upon him) said: 'O Messenger of Allah! A group of people came to me who had purchased a slave girl, and they all had intercourse with her in one period of purity. So she gave birth to a boy, and they disputed over him, all of them claiming him. So I drew lots among them and assigned him to the one whose lot came out, and I guaranteed their share.' The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'There is no group of people who dispute and then delegate their affair to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, except that the lot of the rightful one comes out.'

key_terms.سَهْمُ الْمُحِقِّ: the lot of the rightful one

ai.seo_question: How did the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) validate the use of drawing lots for resolving paternity disputes in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights Ali ibn Abi Talib’s judicial acumen in Yemen, where he resolved a complex paternity dispute among multiple men who had intercourse with a slave girl during a single period of purity by employing the method of drawing lots (*arba'*). The Prophet Muhammad affirmed this practice, establishing the principle that when a group delegates their claim to Allah through lots, the lot invariably falls upon the rightful party (*al-muḥiqq*), a ruling foundational to Shia jurisprudence for resolving ambiguous claims. This incident underscores the divine guidance inherent in the Ahl al-Bayt’s legal reasoning and the spiritual efficacy of *kura'* (casting lots) as a mechanism for revealing truth.
